title: Why Common Antibiotics Are Failing: The Global Resistance Crisis Explained
excerpt: One in six bacterial infections worldwide now resists treatment, and India — where over-the-counter antibiotic sales remain rampant — faces among the highest resistance rates on the planet.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • One in six bacterial infections globally were resistant to antibiotics in 2023.
  • India had an estimated 297,000 AMR-related deaths in 2019, with rising resistance rates.
  • WHO's Global Action Plan aims for a 10% reduction in AMR deaths by 2030.

  • One in six laboratory-confirmed bacterial infections worldwide were resistant to antibiotics in 2023, with resistance rising in over 40% of monitored pathogen-antibiotic combinations since 2018.
  • India faces a disproportionate burden: AMR caused an estimated 297,000 deaths in 2019, with over-the-counter antibiotic sales and self-medication driving resistance rates far above global averages.
  • WHO has launched a new Global Action Plan on AMR (2026–2036) targeting a 10% reduction in AMR-associated deaths by 2030, while researchers pursue AI-driven drug discovery and bacteriophage therapies.

The Scale of the Crisis

Antibiotic resistance is no longer a distant threat — it is a present-day emergency killing more than a million people annually. According to the World Health Organization's latest data, approximately one in six laboratory-confirmed bacterial infections worldwide were resistant to antibiotic treatments in 2023. Between 2018 and 2023, resistance rose in over 40% of the pathogen-antibiotic combinations WHO monitors, with an average annual increase of 5–15%.

Bacterial AMR was associated with more than 4.7 million deaths globally in 2021, according to a Lancet study. The WHO estimates that drug-resistant infections directly kill 1.2 million people each year and contribute to nearly 5 million additional deaths. If current trends hold, the total cost of treating resistant bacterial infections alone is projected to reach $412 billion annually through 2035, with an additional $443 billion in productivity losses each year.

"We're at a place now where antibiotic resistance is a global crisis. It's killing large numbers of people around the world every day."

— Dr. Helen Boucher, Dean, Tufts University School of Medicine

Why Common Medicines Are Failing

The mechanics of resistance are straightforward: bacteria evolve to survive the drugs designed to kill them. The problem is that human behaviour is accelerating this natural process at an alarming rate. Misuse and overuse of antibiotics — taking them for viral infections like the common cold, not completing prescribed courses, or using them preventively in livestock — give bacteria repeated opportunities to develop defences.

In 2022, so-called "access" antibiotics recommended as first-choice treatments accounted for only 53% of global human antibiotic use, according to WHO. Higher-risk "watch" antibiotics made up roughly 45%, exceeding 70% of total use in nearly one-third of countries — far short of the global target calling for at least 70% of use from the safer access group by 2030.

Drug-resistant gram-negative bacteria, particularly E. coli and K. pneumoniae, are becoming increasingly dangerous in bloodstream infections that can lead to sepsis, organ failure, and death. Ciprofloxacin resistance in gonorrhoea has reached 75% globally, and resistance to ceftriaxone — the last reliable first-line treatment — is rising in multiple regions.

India's Acute Vulnerability

The WHO identifies its South-East Asia Region, which includes India, as having among the highest resistance rates globally — one in three reported infections in the region were resistant to treatment. India's specific burden is staggering.

A 2026 review published in Frontiers in Antibiotics found that multidrug-resistant infections in India carry a 13.1% mortality rate and nearly double treatment costs to $199 per case. An estimated 297,000 deaths in India were attributed to AMR in 2019 alone, a figure projected to reach 2 million annually by 2050. Over 50,000 Indian newborns die each year from sepsis caused by bacteria resistant to first-line antibiotics, according to data cited by the Indian Council of Medical Research.

Several India-specific factors compound the problem. A study of pharmacies in south-central India found that nearly 78% dispensed antibiotics over the counter without a valid prescription, with azithromycin, amoxicillin, and cefixime the most commonly sold. Among those pharmacists dispensing antibiotics without prescriptions, 82.5% were unaware of antimicrobial resistance and its consequences. The cultural practice of sharing leftover medicines within families, combined with incomplete antibiotic courses, further fuels resistance.

ICMR surveillance data underscore the trajectory: E. coli susceptibility to imipenem — a last-resort carbapenem antibiotic — fell from 86% in 2016 to 64% in 2021, while clinical isolates of E. coli in outpatient settings surged from 6,525 in 2018 to 18,995 in 2023.

New Weapons and New Strategies

The pharmaceutical pipeline for new antibiotics has thinned dramatically, with most major companies exiting the field because short-course treatments offer limited returns compared to chronic-disease drugs. The WHO's new Global Action Plan on AMR (2026–2036) aims to reverse this trend, targeting a 10% reduction in AMR-associated deaths by 2030 through coordinated action across human, animal, and environmental health sectors.

Researchers are pursuing several promising alternatives. Scientists at Nature reported in June 2026 that an AI-powered tool has identified potential antibiotics effective against drug-resistant gonorrhoea. A separate study found that a cocktail of four antibiotic compounds produced by soil bacteria can kill superbugs by attacking multiple points in an essential metabolic pathway. Bacteriophage therapy — using viruses that target specific bacteria — has shown favourable results in a Phase 2 clinical trial for drug-resistant Staphylococcus aureus bloodstream infections.

What Individuals Can Do

Experts emphasise several practical steps: never take antibiotics without a prescription, always complete the full prescribed course, and never share or reuse leftover antibiotics. Vaccination, proper hand hygiene, and safe food handling also reduce infection risk and the need for antibiotics in the first place. For the Indian diaspora, awareness of these practices is particularly important when travelling to or from India, where resistant strains circulate more widely than in many Western countries.

As Dr. Lance Price of George Washington University's Antibiotic Resistance Action Center notes, the stakes extend beyond infectious disease: "Common procedures like C-sections, hip replacements, and prostate biopsies — all of these rely on functional antibiotics to either prevent or treat the infections associated with those procedures." Without effective antibiotics, modern medicine as we know it is at risk.
